::: {.callout-important}
## What We Can Currently Conclude

A swing determines much more than clubhead speed: it sets orientation, angular velocity, impact position, shaft deformation and velocity, internal stress, and the mechanical conditions at the hands. Those states can affect the subsequent collision and vibration. A short contact interval restricts some mechanisms; it does not prove that every shaft or grip effect vanishes.

The earlier version of this article claimed universal 99% decoupling, a universal rigid-shaft bound, and complete isolation of the hands. Those claims are withdrawn. They were not established by the available one-dimensional model or by the cited time-scale arguments. The corrected arithmetic and model boundaries appear below. No player-specific acoustic advantage has yet been established by this project.
:::

## What Does a Heavy or Sweet Hit Mean? {#sec-impact-estimands}

An observer may hear two players strike the same kind of club and describe one strike as more solid. That observation deserves investigation, but it does not identify its cause. Equipment, ball construction, impact position, speed, loft, surface condition, the turf, and the listening position can all differ. Even with those controlled, elastic state and hand contact may differ.

Use separate estimands rather than a single inferred "heaviness":

| Question | Observable | Necessary Qualification |
|---|---|---|
| How much momentum reaches the ball? | Contact impulse vector $\mathbf J=\int\mathbf F_c\,dt$ | Subtract other ball impulses if material |
| How much energy reaches the ball? | Change in translational and rotational kinetic energy | Include initial ball motion and spin |
| How does the face move during contact? | Head recoil, rotation, local deformation, contact duration | Full inertia and contact geometry |
| What reaches the hands? | Three-axis acceleration, force/torque spectra and ringdown | Sensor location, bandwidth and grip state |
| What reaches a listener? | Calibrated pressure waveform and spectrum | Microphone position, directivity and room response |
| What sounds or feels sweet? | Blinded preference and discrimination ratings | Population, stimulus level and experimental protocol |

Smash factor is a speed ratio, not a measurement of body mass coupled to the collision. Peak force, impulse, ball energy, shaft strain energy and acoustic energy are distinct. In particular, a change in sound can be perceptible without a practically important change in ball speed.

There is also no unique mechanical sweet spot. Maximum ball speed, minimum head rotation, a center of percussion for a specified support, minimum excitation of a selected mode, minimum hand vibration and preferred sound can occur at different face positions. A mode's node is not automatically the optimum for every mode or every boundary condition.

## Evidence That Sets the Scope {#sec-impact-evidence}

The historical free-head approximation is a useful baseline, not an unrestricted theorem. In a flexible-club study, McNally, McPhee and Henrikson compared full-club and detached-head impacts and found altered launch and gear effect. The shaft stiffness was fitted, contact calibration used near-center strikes, and the wider face maps extend beyond that calibration region. This supports investigating coupling, not importing a universal percentage into our software [@mcnally2018shaftimpact].

Corke and colleagues investigated strain propagation in a clamped steel-shafted 9-iron using incoming balls, motivated by robot-grip validity. Their grip-reflection result supports a limited influence of the remote clamp during that tested collision. It does not remove the local shaft, pre-existing loads, or all composite-shaft configurations [@corke2018gripping]. These studies address different mechanisms and need not contradict each other.

Milne and Davis combined swing simulation with shaft-strain measurements; MacKenzie and Boucher investigated changes in delivered kinematics with shaft stiffness. Both belong in the pre-impact evidence base. Neither alone identifies a grip-dependent acoustic mechanism [@milne1992shaft; @mackenzie2017shaft]. Brown and McPhee's club–grip study provides a further reason to identify a compliant boundary rather than assume a clamp [@brown2018grip].

The detailed [review ledger](https://github.com/D-sorganization/AffineDrift/blob/docs/4253-impact-dynamics-acoustics/docs/development/impact-acoustics/REVIEW.md) distinguishes full-text inspection, abstract-only evidence, independent derivation, and proposed experiments. The [capability inventory](https://github.com/D-sorganization/AffineDrift/blob/docs/4253-impact-dynamics-acoustics/docs/development/impact-acoustics/INVENTORY.md) links software claims to source and tests.

## Rigid-Body Contact Is a Reference, Not the Whole Model {#sec-impact-mobility}

Let $\mathbf r$ point from the head center of mass to the contact point, $m_h$ be head mass, and $\mathbf I_h$ be its full inertia tensor about its center of mass. All quantities use one orthonormal frame. For an impulse $\mathbf j$ **on the head**,

$$
\Delta\mathbf v_h=\frac{\mathbf j}{m_h},\qquad
\Delta\boldsymbol\omega_h=\mathbf I_h^{-1}(\mathbf r\times\mathbf j).
$$

The instantaneous change of contact-point velocity is therefore

$$
\Delta\mathbf v_c=\mathbf W_h\mathbf j,\qquad
\mathbf W_h=\frac{\mathbf 1}{m_h}-[\mathbf r]_\times\mathbf I_h^{-1}[\mathbf r]_\times.
$$ {#eq-impact-point-mobility}

Here $[\mathbf r]_\times\mathbf a=\mathbf r\times\mathbf a$. The rotational contribution is positive semidefinite: for a unit normal $\mathbf n$,

$$
\frac{1}{m_{h,n}}=\mathbf n^T\mathbf W_h\mathbf n
=\frac{1}{m_h}+(\mathbf r\times\mathbf n)^T\mathbf I_h^{-1}(\mathbf r\times\mathbf n).
$$ {#eq-impact-normal-mass}

This retains products of inertia and orientation. The familiar $1/m_h+r^2/I$ is a special principal-axis case. An offset parallel to the normal produces no normal-impulse moment. Off-diagonal point mobility can nevertheless couple a normal impulse to tangential contact velocity.

For two detached bodies, add their point inverse-mass matrices: $\mathbf W=\mathbf W_h+\mathbf W_b$. Let $u_n>0$ denote normal closing speed, including both linear and angular point velocities. The frictionless Newton-restitution reference is

$$
J_n=\frac{(1+e)u_n}{\mathbf n^T\mathbf W\mathbf n},\qquad 0\le e\le1.
$$ {#eq-impact-normal-impulse}

The ball receives $+J_n\mathbf n$ and the head receives $-J_n\mathbf n$. For a sphere with normal through its center, its normal inverse mass is $1/m_b$. With no other impulses, loss of kinetic energy is

$$
E^- - E^+=\frac12\frac{(1-e^2)u_n^2}{\mathbf n^T\mathbf W\mathbf n}.
$$

Thus an eccentric strike can reduce ball launch and increase head rotation even when head speed is unchanged. It is not generally valid to infer the total system's effective mass by fitting a single scalar to launch data: restitution, friction, local face compliance and unmeasured initial states can compensate for each other.

For multibody generalized velocities $\dot{\mathbf q}$ with mass matrix $\mathbf M$ and contact Jacobian $\mathbf J_c$, the corresponding unconstrained point inverse mass is $\mathbf J_c\mathbf M^{-1}\mathbf J_c^T$. If the selected model imposes bilateral velocity constraints $\mathbf A\dot{\mathbf q}=0$, use the constrained inverse operator

$$
\mathbf M_c^{-1}=\mathbf M^{-1}-\mathbf M^{-1}\mathbf A^T
(\mathbf A\mathbf M^{-1}\mathbf A^T)^{-1}\mathbf A\mathbf M^{-1}
$$

on an independent constraint set, then form $\mathbf J_c\mathbf M_c^{-1}\mathbf J_c^T$. Singular or redundant constraints require an explicitly documented reduction. A rigid constraint acts instantaneously by model definition; that does not demonstrate instantaneous propagation through a physical shaft.

The directional effective mass is $1/(\mathbf n^T\mathbf W\mathbf n)$, **not** $\mathbf n^T\mathbf W^{-1}\mathbf n$. The latter corresponds to a different condition when tangential motion is constrained. A normal restitution rule combined with friction must solve coupled normal/tangential contact consistently; independently clipping a tangential impulse need not preserve restitution or passivity.

For frictional contact, retain ball and head spin, face curvature, local contact normal, tangential compliance and a stick/slip law. Gear effect is an outcome of rotation and tangential interaction. Adding a separate empirical gear-effect correction to a solver that already resolves it can double-count the mechanism. See the companion [impact mechanics reference](impact-mechanics-and-ball-flight.html).

## Contact Time, Wave Transit, and the Limits of a Scaling Law {#sec-impact-timescales}

Driver contact is commonly discussed on a sub-millisecond scale, but contact duration is an equipment- and speed-dependent measurement, not a universal constant [@roberts2001contacttime]. Distinguish the duration $T_c$, local head-mode periods, shaft wave travel, grip reflection, and the much longer decay heard or felt after separation.

For a uniform slender rod, the elementary axial approximation is $c=\sqrt{E/\rho}$. With the earlier article's *assumed* steel values, $E=210$ GPa and $\rho=7850$ kg/m³, this gives approximately 5172 m/s. A 1.15 m shaft then has one-way transit 222 microseconds and round-trip transit 445 microseconds. It is incorrect to say the wave has not reached the hands by 450 microseconds.

The earlier assumed composite inputs $E=90$–150 GPa and $\rho=1500$–1600 kg/m³ imply 7500–10000 m/s within that rod approximation, not 3800–4500 m/s. Corresponding 1.15 m round trips are approximately 230–307 microseconds. Actual tapered, anisotropic laminates require measured or derived branch-specific wave speeds, coupling, attenuation and reflection coefficients. These arithmetic examples establish neither negligible coupling nor a large effect.

For a uniform Euler–Bernoulli beam with mass per length $\mu$,

$$
\omega=\sqrt{EI/\mu}\,k^2,\qquad
v_g=2(EI/\mu)^{1/4}\sqrt{\omega}.
$$

Flexural wave speed is dispersive. This low-frequency beam theory is not a causal high-frequency wavefront model; its unbounded group speed at arbitrarily high frequency marks its breakdown. Rayleigh, Timoshenko or three-dimensional elasticity is needed where rotary inertia, shear or local head/hosel wavelengths matter. One flexural transit estimate cannot bound axial, torsional and coupled branches simultaneously.

A delayed reflection from the hands is only one pathway. The shaft close to the hosel responds immediately; shaft stress and motion already present at contact need no newly launched round trip. Neural feedback triggered by impact is also a different mechanism from pre-existing activation and passive grip impedance.

### What the Small-Time Expansion Actually Says

Over a sufficiently short interval, with smooth finite non-contact loading and fixed configuration to leading order,

$$
\mathbf M_0\Delta\dot{\mathbf q}
=\mathbf J_{c,0}^T\mathbf J+\int_0^{T_c}\boldsymbol\tau_{\rm ext}\,dt+O(T_c).
$$

The remainder includes appropriately bounded drift and configuration variation; it is not a universal numerical error certificate. A bounded torque produces an $O(T_c)$ angular impulse. Converting it to ball impulse requires the system Jacobian and constraints, not an arbitrary division by a club length.

In an initially relaxed lumped spring, a finite collision-induced velocity change gives an incremental displacement $O(T_c)$. Spring force is then $O(kT_c)$ and its accumulated impulse is $O(kT_c^2)$. This is the restricted origin of the observed quadratic trend in the Tools fixture. A damper driven by an $O(1)$ velocity change instead gives an $O(cT_c)$ impulse; pre-existing spring force also contributes $O(T_c)$. A rigid constraint is a different, singular limit. Varying contact stiffness while keeping contact damping fixed also changes restitution. Therefore a fitted quadratic trend is not a law for every grip, shaft, load history and collision law.

Useful dimensionless comparisons include $k_sT_c^2/m_h$, $c_sT_c/m_h$, $\omega_jT_c$, branch-specific round-trip time divided by $T_c$, and shaft-to-contact dynamic impedance. Report their ranges with the quantities held fixed.

### Two Other Corrections to the Former Argument

The earlier rigid-arm example gives

$$
\frac{(4.5\,\mathrm{kg})(0.65\,\mathrm m)^2/3}{(1.8\,\mathrm m)^2}
=0.1956\,\mathrm{kg},
$$

not 7.5 g. This is the arm contribution for that artificial common-pivot geometry; a real articulated assembly needs its actual mass matrix. A shaft segment not spanning the whole pivot-to-tip radius also needs its actual parallel-axis contribution. Neither calculation supplies a universal rigid-shaft upper bound. Prestored elastic energy, contact dynamics, resonance and different boundary conditions can invalidate an assumed monotone ordering with stiffness.

Force, impulse and duration must also agree. A half-sine pulse satisfies $J=2F_{\max}T_c/\pi$. Choosing $J=3$ N s and $T_c=450$ microseconds gives $F_{\max}=10.47$ kN. These are illustrative consistent inputs, not measured peak-force limits.

## Dynamic Stiffening and Applied Wrenches {#sec-impact-prestress}

A tensile load increases transverse restoring force geometrically; it need not change the material's Young modulus. A small-deflection beam under a declared axial tension $N(s,t)$ has the structural terms

$$
\mu w_{tt}+(EIw_{ss})_{ss}-(Nw_s)_s=f_\perp.
$$ {#eq-impact-tension-beam}

For admissible displacement $w$, the tensile geometric energy is $\tfrac12\int_0^L Nw_s^2\,ds$. The finite-element geometric stiffness is

$$
(\mathbf K_g)_{ij}=\int_0^L N(s)\phi_i'(s)\phi_j'(s)\,ds.
$$

For nonnegative tension this contribution is positive semidefinite. Compression changes the sign and can lead to instability. Natural frequencies follow the loaded eigenproblem, with the same head inertia and grip boundary used in the dynamics; a scalar factor $1+N/P_{cr}$ is only a declared reduction.

In a straight radial beam rotating steadily with angular speed $\Omega$, root offset $R_0$, tip mass $m_h$, and no additional axial loads,

$$
N(s)=m_h\Omega^2(R_0+L)+\int_s^L\mu(\xi)\Omega^2(R_0+\xi)\,d\xi.
$$

This is a useful verification case, not the tension distribution of every three-dimensional golf swing. As an illustrative scale, $m_h=0.2$ kg, $\Omega=40$ rad/s and tip radius 1.2 m give a 384 N tip centrifugal load. Determine the actual time-dependent force/moment field from the swing, including head CG eccentricity, distributed shaft inertia, base acceleration and constraints.

In coordinates rotating with the shaft base,

$$
\mathbf a=\mathbf a_0+\mathbf R\left[
\ddot{\boldsymbol\rho}+2\boldsymbol\Omega\times\dot{\boldsymbol\rho}
+\dot{\boldsymbol\Omega}\times\boldsymbol\rho
+\boldsymbol\Omega\times(\boldsymbol\Omega\times\boldsymbol\rho)\right].
$$

Coriolis terms depend on motion relative to the rotating frame. In an appropriate linearized conservative system they produce a skew-symmetric gyroscopic matrix, not material stiffness or viscous damping. The identity $\dot{\boldsymbol\eta}^T\mathbf G\dot{\boldsymbol\eta}=0$ for $\mathbf G^T=-\mathbf G$ is an energy test. Centrifugal prestress can stiffen bending, while other rotational terms can soften or split modes depending on geometry. Derive all terms from one kinetic/potential-energy formulation to avoid counting rotation twice. Rotating-beam literature supplies mathematical comparison cases, not golf calibration [@rodrigues2024spinning].

For a reduced model about a declared loaded trajectory, a schematic form is

$$
\mathbf M\ddot{\boldsymbol\eta}+(\mathbf C+\mathbf G)\dot{\boldsymbol\eta}
+(\mathbf K_e+\mathbf K_g+\mathbf K_{\rm rot})\boldsymbol\eta
=\mathbf B_c\mathbf F_c+\mathbf B_g\mathbf w_g+\mathbf f_{\rm base}.
$$ {#eq-impact-modal-system}

A time-varying reduction also needs its basis-derivative terms. Head shell/face modes, shaft axial/bending/torsional modes, and the hosel connection must be retained or condensed with demonstrated bandwidth accuracy. Contact forces and grip wrenches act at specified positions; a wrench shifted to another origin obeys $\mathbf M_O=\mathbf M_P+(\mathbf p_P-\mathbf p_O)\times\mathbf F$.

For each grip, power is $P_g=\mathbf F_g\cdot\mathbf v_g+\mathbf M_g\cdot\boldsymbol\omega_g$ using colocated conjugate quantities. Compare ongoing wrench application with preloaded strain energy and delivered motion separately. Setting motor torque to zero does not erase stored elastic energy, damping or an already established constraint. Under [the notation contract](../NOTATION.md), a zero-torque counterfactual sets only the declared controls to zero; it must retain the specified plant and initial state.

A mechanically meaningful energy audit is

$$
E_{\rm mech}(t)+E_{\rm diss}(0,t)+E_{\rm rad}(0,t)
=E_{\rm mech}(0)+\int_0^t P_{\rm boundary}\,dt,
$$

with every retained energy and boundary defined. If acoustic back-reaction is neglected, do not subtract estimated acoustic energy a second time from an independently damped structural simulation. The approximation and its error must be declared.
